review: After the latest patch that added "classic" combat setting I've made more progress in a single session than during past 2 days worth of playtime on "challenging" ("Hard") difficulty. The game is infinitely more enjoyable now, and plays just as expected from Darksiders title - fluid, fast and fun. I highly recommend buying this game If you were previously concerned about the difficulty or the technical issues. Most of them are fixed now, and developers truly deserve our support for listening to the community and reacting fast.

So I managed to get every achievement for this game, and I think I can safely say that this game is the worst in the franchise so far.  Most people whine that it's too hard, and yes, Apocalyptic difficulty will give you gray hairs.  For being one of the horsemen, Fury is pathetically weak and can be two or three shotted by the early game enemies.  But that's not really why this game doesn't match up to the previous installments.

First of all, this game feels broken.  The main mechanic of the game, Fury's dodge, seems to work about 80% of the time.  There were many times where I felt I should have activated it, but it just didn't.  I thought it might have been an issue with my controller, but I don't have this problem in any of my other games, not to mention that the same thing happens with Fury's jump.  Sometimes, the control just doesn't respond at all and you wind up falling and taking a big health hit.  Everything else is responsive, so I'm pretty convinced that it's something in the games programming, but given the fact that the dodge has this problem is unacceptable.  

Then there's numerous other bugs that I encountered over and over again.  Several times, I got Fury out of bounds even though I wasn't actually trying to do that.  Even though I didn't fall through the world, I somehow managed to go above it with no way back. This meant I had to forcefully restart and sacrifice all the souls I collected.  Was annoying and really something that should have been patched, but looks like it never will be.

The real problem with this game is that it just wants to copy Dark Souls without keeping any of the elements that made the previous installments successful.  Gone are the tricky puzzles, maps, dungeons, items, treasure chests, and skill trees.  Instead, fury gets 4 items throughout the entire game called hollows.  Each hollow gives you a new ability and a new weapon.  So you get 4 additional abilities and 4 additional weapons plus a boomerang which is useless in combat.  The amount of content in this game is laughable.  Unless you're an achievement hunter, expect to spend around 10-15 hours on your main play through, and for that play through, expect to die A LOT.  Of that 10-15 hours, you can probably expect 6 of them to be retries of the areas you continue to die on.

It's not all bad.  The stuff that's actually enjoyable is the DLC, which means the good stuff is behind a pay wall.  The keepers of the void content was pretty awesome and actually had a bit of the feel that previous games offered.  It's pretty much the only dungeon like area you will get to traverse through.  The crucible is back as well, but I never really found that to be something to write home about.  That is just OK.  Fury's whip gives a Castlevania feel which is a nice touch.

But overall, I was really disappointed.  I loved the first two games, but this one was nothing more than a giant dumpster fire.  I'm really hoping that Genesis brings the game back to the roots, but we'll have to see what is done with it.
I'm never listening to reviews again. Look, if you think a game will interest you and be awesome, THEN TRY IT OUT. DO NOT LISTEN TO YOUTUBERS OR REVIEWS. This game is F***ing amazing.

Darksiders III — Review
Darksiders III is an action-adventure game starring Fury, one of the Four Horsemen of the Apocalypse. Her mission is to hunt down the Seven Deadly Sins across a ruined, hostile world.
Fury fights with a whip and a range of magical forms, each offering different attacks and ways to explore. Combat rewards patience and careful timing, giving the game a more deliberate feel than its predecessors. The interconnected world is full of hidden paths, dangerous enemies, and environmental puzzles.
The game’s dark fantasy art and atmospheric soundtrack create a memorable setting, and Fury’s sharp personality gives the story plenty of character. However, the combat can feel unforgiving, and some encounters become repetitive. Exploration and backtracking may also test your patience.
Verdict: Darksiders III offers a stylish, challenging adventure with a compelling lead and a distinctive world. It’s best suited to players who enjoy deliberate combat and dark fantasy exploration.

Main Differences Between Darksiders III and Previous Games

1. Gameplay Style

Darksiders I & II: More traditional hack-and-slash with light RPG elements. Open world with lots of loot and puzzles.
Darksiders III: Leans more towards a "Souls-like" experience – slower, more deliberate combat, with dodging and timing being more important.

2. Combat Mechanics

Darksiders I & II: Combo-heavy combat, with multiple weapons and flashy moves.
Darksiders III: Simplified combat system focusing on dodges and counterattacks. Less weapon variety, but more emphasis on tactical fighting.

3. Character and Story

Darksiders I: You play as War.
Darksiders II: You play as Death.
Darksiders III: You play as Fury, the third Horseman (or Horsewoman). Her personality is more aggressive and impatient compared to War and Death.

4. World Design

Darksiders I & II: More open-world and exploratory, especially Darksiders II with its large maps and side quests.
Darksiders III: Metroidvania-style world – interconnected areas that unlock with new abilities. More linear but interconnected, like Dark Souls.

5. Loot and RPG Elements

Darksiders II: Heavy on loot, gear upgrades, and skill trees.
Darksiders III: Minimal loot. Focus is on upgrading a few core weapons and abilities. More streamlined.

6.Checkpoint and Save System

Darksiders I & II: Manual save points or frequent autosaves.
Darksiders III: Uses Souls-like checkpoints (Serpent Holes) where you respawn after death, and enemies reset.

7. Puzzle Design

Darksiders I & II: Focused more on Zelda-style dungeons, full of environmental puzzles.
Darksiders III: Less puzzle-heavy. Puzzles exist but are simpler and fewer, with more focus on platforming and combat.

8. Mount

Darksiders I & II : gave players an epic feeling of being a Horseman, thanks in part to their powerful mounts.
Darksiders III : Fury doesn’t have a horse, which disappointed many fans, especially since she is also one of the Four Horsemen.

 9.Tone and Atmosphere

Darksiders III: Darker and more mature tone, with a stronger emphasis on atmosphere and mystery.
Earlier games were more comic book-like and colorful.

I'll keep this in bullet points for brevity:

[b]The good[/b]
[list]
[*]Beautiful world, and a very well-rendered character even if her armor is a bit... well... either under- or overdone, can't decide which it is.
[*]Impacts when you punch things feel meaty enough to make hits enjoyable.
[*]Removed the horrible loot system from Darksiders 2.
[*]The sins are all visually well-designed.
[*]Voiceovers for the most part are decent.
[/list]

[b]The bad[/b]
[list]
[*]As pretty as many areas are, some are drab, and given the game uses a low-fi approach to its design coupled with pretty areas when those end up not-pretty, the game looks really bad.
[*]You can't block. The enemies can. You have few interrupting sweeping attacks. The enemies do. But you're one of the four horsemen fighting grunts? Uh huh. Grunts who kill you in 3 hits? Uh huh. The gameplay totally doesn't mirror the story/setting as if this had been a different game until late in development.
[*]Telegraphic / backside indicators are so marginal they might as well not exist. This was updated and while marginally better, I feel this is still far from what it ought to be. Many attacks don't telegraph their moment of hit at all, for example.
[*]Menu system is super weird. Seemingly random key assignments. Lots of unnecessary busywork like constantly breaking clusters for currency in your inventory.
[*]Different consumables which due to the speed of combat and the controller-centric controls are mostly pointless and can freely be sold for currency. You don't have time to select/use them properly mid-fight, anyhow.
[*]A level-up system which is pointless and should have been scrapped for purity of design.
[*]The game is chock-full of cheap shots. Archers placed higher than the camera pans and too far to hear the sounds, no-windup attacks which interrupt you and have no tell, jumping enemies coming from the back with a reach greater than the backside indicators, such stuff.
[/list]

[b]The ugly[/b]
[list]
[*]A central part is the combat, which takes up a good 90%+ of the gameplay. Sadly, it's also the weakest part, struggling with a lack of balance in something which needs to be finely tweaked because they made the player character really, really frail. The update made easier difficulties somewhat easier, but it's still really weird and doesn't feel like you're playing a mighty horse(wo)man. Sadly.
[*]The combat is also quite boring because of the imbalance between different attack damage outputs. In the end you spam dodge until you get a perfect dodge (the window is tiny but you'll get it every so often), then press LMB to counterattack. You repeat this until the boss dies or you fall asleep, usually the latter. When Fury muses in the opening whether you can die from boredom, I didn't think she'd be talking about the combat system :(
[*]Enemies surround you frequently, yet your dodge is one of physical avoidance with only ~1/10th of a second of invulnerability, and no AE counterattack. The gameplay is entirely built for 1v1 combat, yet the levels usually place you in group fights like the old Darksiders games.
[*]It commits the deadly sin of Badly Placed Waypoints Forcing You To Run Back 5 Minutes Through Empty Rooms. Gaming as a whole solved this 20-25 years ago. Get with the times, devs!
[*]It feels nothing like Darksiders. At all
[/list]

[b]"What were they thinking?"[/b] - this is the question that raced through my mind about 70% of the playtime of this game.
I loved Darksiders 1. I loved Darksiders 2.
I could barely get the will together to finish Darksiders 3.

[b]The Good[/b]
It's not a terrible game, it really isn't.
The graphics are as nice as they were in the last two games.
The story is also as good and finally answers some questions that have been on people's minds since the last two games (no, not all questions, don't worry).
The voice acting, sounds, all good.
And this is why I would recommend this to people who played Darksiders 1 + 2, if they have a lot of patience for BS gameplay. You won't be disappointed by story, graphics or audio.
And thankfully, the game isn't that long so you won't have to chew through the gameplay for days...

[b]Everything else is a complete mess[/b]
And the worst part? Pretty much every downside of this game was totally avoidable, totally unnecessary - other games, including this game's own prequels, did it better.

They changed the gameplay in an obvious attempt to cash in on the Dark Souls hype. Which would have been fine, if they had done it right. But they didn't.
While War and Death felt like the awesome entities they are supposed to be, Fury plays like a fragile weakling for almost the entire game. Enemies dish out absurd amounts of damage and the only thing you can do about it is dodge, dodge, dodge,... see where Dark Souls come in?

The problem is that Dark Souls works because both normal enemies and bosses telegraph their attacks in just the right way, not too obvious, not too subtle. In Darksiders 3, almost every enemy is either unreadable or an open book.
Hitboxes are also a mess. Attacks that really shouldn't hit you do - and vice versa.

But your biggest enemy is not something with an HP bar. It is the camera.
You are too zoomed in almost the entire time. Fury's admittedly pretty back is just in your way all the time. The vast majority of your time, you fight multiple enemies, but can only see 1 or 2 of them at once. 
The rest does something behind your back that you can't see, hear or defend against properly - forcing you to go on the most absurd dodging-sprees in recent gaming history. And you'll still die a ton.
As if that wasn't enough, the tiny bit of the fight you CAN see will become obstructed by your own effects. Good luck seeing anything when the entire screen is filled with fire, lightning, etc...

I am not lying when I say that 70-80% of my deaths were down to the camera and complete lack of overview in combat.

And there's more:
The game's "RPG" part is unbalanced. With the enemies hitting so hard, health is a complete dump stat. Put no more than 10 points into it, the rest into physical and/or arcane.
The progression is also unbalanced - at the beginning, the game is very hard. Near the end, everything is a pushover.
There is no map. Good luck looking for humans when going back to previous areas.
YOU CANNOT CHANGE THE CONTROLLER LAYOUT (WTF?! IN 2019?!) - and the default layout is weird as hell. 
Only two puzzles in the game got me thinking, the rest is just too easy. And I suck at puzzles.

This is one of those times I wished that steam had a sliding scale for a review instead of a simple yes or no. Anyway, where do we start with Darksiders 3?

I played the first two games, and while I didn't absolutely go nuts for them, they were quite fun to play. Although the original Darksiders 1 shows its age (not sure about the remastered edition), Darksiders 2 was absolutely fine. It's something that is not too terrible, and also actually enjoy playing. Needless to say, I was engaged enough to look forward to Darksiders 3.

And boy, was I met with disappointment and frustration. The game changed genre - from being more of a fun exploration with occasional tough fights - to a wannabe Dark Souls. In the previous two games, after playing a bit of the game, you become powerful enough to not worry about the general enemies in the game (at least on normal difficulty). In fact, it was quite fun to crush everything in your path while exploring the world. You are met with the occasional boss fights for that extra challenge, but nothing you can't handle. After all, you are one of the four legendary, all powerful, horseman. Turning to Darksiders 3, I am more than half way through the game, and I have to obsessively watch my health bar since even two or three normal enemies can easily kill you.

Story: Story wise it is similar to the other two games - nothing super deep - but enough to get you going. However, I do not expect a really deep story from this franchise, so I don't particularly mind. Fury is an interesting enough character to make you care.

Graphics: Inconsistent and disappointing given the release date. Even maxing everything, only a few areas look good. However, you can clearly spot areas that are really visually poor - for instance acid or water. This is in contrast with some cave areas which looked pretty decent. The character model is borderline okay, but I would have preferred to see better visual fidelity. On my RX580, the frame rates fell below 60FPS at 1440p, which is quite disappointing for the graphical quality it offers. This maybe indicative of a poor port.

Combat: I had several issues with combat. First off, as I mentioned, the difficulty is massively scaled in this game. Almost all of the time, the only viable strategy is to dodge and counter. Most enemies block or dodge your chain attacks fairly easily. There are very few occasions where you can unleash any sort of chain combos at all, making me wonder why they even exist. This makes combat really tiring and uninteresting - which is a shame as that was one of the main points about the franchise. 

Fighting one enemy is okay, but often you are faced with hordes of enemies, which is honestly quite bad since you can really only focus on one enemy at a time. So you may get attacked from outside your field of view, potentially ending the encounter pretty quickly.

In the previous two games, chaos form did significant damage and makes you an unstoppable and fearful force. You could crush almost everything in your path. In this game? It's crap, weak. It no longer feels like an unstoppable force, but more like a temporary invincibility that can be used in a pinch. The damage is so lame, you might as well not bother with it. 

Weapons, upgrades and collectables: There are a fixed number of weapons in the game, your base weapon - a whip, and few others that you acquire through out the story. Unlike Darksiders 2, there are no weapon drops and instead, the focus is on upgrading these weapons. Unfortunately, you cannot upgrade all of them entirely, so you have to choose at most a couple of weapons to focus on. It can get quite boring after a while since you will stick to one or two weapons for most of the game and have no incentive to try out different weapons. The materials required to upgrade is found throughout the world, so exploration generally pays off. Souls act both as currency and level up material. I am not particularly a fan of tying levels to souls.

Mechanics: The mechanics are not fluid or consistent at all. For instance, it is important to lock on to an enemy this game to ensure that you can dodge properly. But, the enemies move around a lot, and the camera loses focus almost as quickly as you lock onto them. This means that through out a battle, you will have to keep trying to lock onto the enemy several times, which makes it extremely cumbersome. Then, the key presses are never properly registered. For instance, I was unable to dodge and immediately heal, or dodge and immediately activate chaos form. It will just ignore the key presses until you fully finish the first action and stop. This is extremely frustrating as when you are in a tight situation, you end up dying since it never registered the vital key press that could have easily saved your life. Oh and when you die, you respawn at a checkpoint and all enemies are also respawned, forcing you to fight all the enemies in the area again, making it rather tedious.

There is no "maps". In the previous game, you had maps and could look up where to go. This game does away with maps entirely. While it's linear enough to not feel like you get lost constantly, there are occasions where it is not entirely clear how to proceed, which makes it somewhat annoying. Overall, I am not too swayed one way or the other on this one.

Soundtrack: Decent, the deluxe edition includes lossless soundtrack, so that's a bonus.

Overall: If you don't mind the souls-like nature of the game and are looking for that kind of combat, then this game may not disappoint you. However, if you are coming from Darksiders 2, then this game maybe quite disappointing from almost every perspective - graphics, mechanics, and (especially) combat. I paid 20$ on sale, and I would recommend waiting until it's even lower - maybe around 10$ for the deluxe game. Look elsewhere until the price drops. 5/10.

Don't let the play time fool you. I played this game on my GOG Galaxy launcher for a very long time. My Review:

This game is a Darksiders game in only 3 aspects: The name, the art style and the story. Let's get that bit out of the way first.

If you are thinking of purchasing this game, hoping it will have the fun combat systems from either the first or the second game, you will be sorely, angrily disappointed.

I'm going to summarize this entire review and then dig in and explain: This isn't a Darksiders game as much as it is a dodge and counter simulator.

If you played the first Darksiders, you probably remember that the dodge was a useful mechanic; not necessary, but useful.

Or maybe you remember Darksiders II, where the dodge mechanic was more central, allowing for counters that were rewarding... again, useful and a little more central, but not game breaking.

But in this game, Dodge+Counter is the ONLY mechanic. The reward is you get to hit them once; the punishment is that even the lowest level enemies will wipe your health to zero in no time. 

Other drawbacks:

- Every enemy attack is an interrupt. What this means is that if the enemy attacks while you are attacking, their attack gets priority, even if you connect; your actions will be interrupted and theirs will often not be. The end result: You die instead of them dying.
- Health items and other consumables are no longer instant use, instead they rely on an overly long animation that can be interrupted. Congratulations, you died. Again.
- If a health/item use animation is interrupted, you don't get the health or bonus, you take the hit. Congratulations, you died. Again.
- *Tested, known to be true*: If an enemy hit will not wipe your actual health # to zero, but put you at less than 20, you die anyway. Yeah, you read that right. Congratulations, you died. Again.
- Primary attack is also the swingline button, so roughly 60-70% of the time, when you jump and attempt to swingline from appropriate objects, the game will register it incorrectly and Fury will perform an air attack instead of a chain swing. About 30% of those times, you will fall to your death. Congratulations, you died. Yet again.
- There is no Save option in the menu, the game only saves whenever you enter an area and pass close to the Vulgrim station; if for some reason you don't get close enough to Vulgrim for him to emerge from his plinth, you don't get a save point.
- If you complete a portion of an area (say, a path to a mini boss or actual boss fight) but die before the next Vulgrim location, you will have to re-battle your way through the entire zone, as all of the enemies respawn. In addition, you lose all of the souls you've collected and haven't spent -> The only upside to this is that the lost souls will all be floating as a soul-head that you can attack to recover your stuff, but one questions whether or not this should be necessary in the first place. Congratulations on your newest death in a long, long, ridiculously long conga-line of deaths.
- There are no more specific Wrath moves, so combat is super simplistic; in short, very Un-Darksiders like.
- There is only 1 wrath bar. It gets completely drained in 1 wrath attack.
- Wrath is incredibly difficult to build.
- Wrath moves do very, very little damage to enemies, even ones of very low levels.
- Chaos form looks cool but is a joke. Remember the days when saving your Chaos form meant wrecking a boss character's face? Not anymore; you'll barely scratch their health bar. Back to the grindy, bull-sugar dodge/counter system for you, ignorant peon.
- Cars and other large environment objects are destructible... but only when Fury is in Chaos form.
- Fury can't pick up or throw cars, a trait both of her horsemen brothers share. For all of the "girl powah" overtones in this game, given the list so far, this results in Fury feeling and playing like a mushy creampuff. In some cases, like in the Lust+Usiel bossfight, you might actually do better in the boss battle if you literally threw a creampuff at the screen (the creampuff being tougher in composition than this laughable excuse for a horseman, Fury).
- Remember the maps from the first 2 games that gave you an idea where you were in the world and where you needed to be going? Not anymore, you don't. You're a peon; worthless, creampuffed horseman scum; no map for you, die where you are, confused, angry and alone.
- Remember the Abyssal Armor from the first 2 games that fully unlocked your horseman abilities and made your character a god-like juggernaught? No you don't; that was all just a dream. Everyone knows the abyssal armor is now locked behind a pay-wall for a DLC that hasn't even been released yet. Get out your wallet, worthless peon.

Remember when Darksiders games were fun, jaunty excursions into a weird, post-apocalyptic world where the combat was central, puzzles existed and occasionally challenged you and dodge was a thing you occasionally did to avoid some damage, not the only mechanic? Remember when Darksiders games were actually FUN?

Not anymore, you don't.

To start I've been a pretty big Darksiders fan since 1, 1 being my favorite so far. Was unsure about 3 so waited a bit to buy it.

The story in this game isn't quite as good as the previous entries though familiar old faces are in it. The main character is alright though feels quite weak in comparison to the Death or War. This is to the detriment of the story and overall feel of the game. I really love the character design I just wish she had more impact in combat. Power fantasy is what i'm looking for and i'm not finding it here, death by a thousand cuts instead. If Fury is really supposed to be full power here then she is significantly weaker than her brothers. The comedy they try to cram in there can get pretty horrible.

The previous two games had you feeling like a major power in the universe, you crushed your enemies. In this game basic skeleton #13 can hit you and take half your life and also shrug off your attacks and swing through them to hit you for that damage. You get staggered by every enemy hit. I've tried both classic and default combat modes and neither feels very good. You dodge and counter, until power up mode then you hit x. (not my cup of tea at all though some like this stuff)

The game wants you to parry/dodge even the smallest minion, some designer really liked dark souls, or maybe the idea of it because it's questionable whether or not they had played one. When you die you drop souls that then have to be recovered! When you die you need to run back to the boss room from a sometimes poorly placed checkpoint through respawned enemies! Enemies are large lumbering brutes that ignore your attacks and require you to do 1 thing wait... and dodge. Tight corridors and a horrible performing camera/lock on system to boot. Do you like the dark souls experience of being killed by off screen enemies that are camera culled or placed where you cant see them because the camera is so limited/clunky? then you may love this.

Did we need estus flask healing system? what was wrong with crushing heads for health?

So far imo this game borrows too much from dark souls and not enough from it's previous entries or god of war. Even if you're going that route at least copy the souls combat competently, this is some sort of mash up that doesn't ever feel good. It does not feed into the unstoppable force fantasy the series is known for, that's for sure. Some of the puzzles thus far have been alright, nothing terribly cinematic like Darksiders 2 though. Where is the unstoppable Nephilim killing machine? This horsemen wants to lead when she is inferior to Death in every way and doesn't feel anywhere near as powerful as War.

I'll finish it for the sake of the series but I am enjoying this a lot less than I had hoped to. I may update my review in future when I finish it if it changes my mind otherwise it will stay as is.

TLDR : This entry is not the adult style Hack and slash with Zelda puzzles you played the last 2 times, it's some other messy beast.

I'm a huge fan of the darksiders franchise am enjoying this game immensely and I honestly don't understand what all of the fuss is about how the game doesn't feel like the 1&2. First of all, that's the point. Each horseman is different and their games reflect that. 

Darksiders 1 you play as War, a walking tank, needing nothing but his strength and giant sword to slash through enemies

Darksiders 2 you play as Death, who plays like a rogue. Quick movements and combining different combos and abilities together to quickly take down opponents. Coupled with his weapon "The Harvester" which takes the form of whatever weapon he wants which allowed a loot system that was not meant to be a staple of the games.

Darksiders 3 you play as Fury, a glass canon. Able to put out a lot of damage but can't take much in return, relying on her quick movement to dodge.

Darksiders 4 if it gets made you'll play as Strife and it's going to be a hell of a lot different. He's a gunslinger who doesn't use that much melee. Are you people complaining about Fury playing differently than Death going to complain about Strife playing differently? It's going to probably end up as a 3rd person action-shooter.

But really, the combat for all of them is very similar, heavily combo based, you just have to be more careful in 3, you can't go in button mashing with you eyes closed. Yes the game is much harder than the first two but it's not unfair, I've yet to encounter a death that made me think "BS", they all feel like my own fault for being impatient or not paying attention.

As for the linear playstyle of the game I adore it. Every single game now adays feels like it needs to shoehorn in an open world, crafting system, loot, and rpg mechanics. It's like, I just wanna sit down and play a game for once without having to travel from one side of the world to another for each mission, manage my inventory, and grind levels/mats.

I see a lot of people comparing it to Dark Souls but other than bonfires/Vulgrim and currency and exp being the same thing I don't see the similarities. Like I said the combat feels exactly the same as the the first two.

I also see a lot of people complaining about the dodging. There aren't many iframes, and they get lowered the higher your difficulty is. You also cannot dodge in the middle of attacking and you have to actually CLEAR attack hitboxes, you can't just time your button presses, this isn't a rhythm game, you have to dodge in the right direction AS WELL AS at the right time. As for countering again, you can't just button mash with your eyes closed in this one, if it's unsafe to attack then don't.

As for my complaints I honestly don't have many. The biggest one is that I really am saddened to see how little amount of puzzles there are. In Darksiders 1&2 there were puzzles everywhere, even the bosses were puzzles. Now I have only faced the first 2 bosses at this point so maybe the others bosses are more puzzle like but puzzles are something I wish there was more of. 

I also miss the execution system, seeing those badass animations War and Death pulled off to kill enemies in the most brutal way was very satisfying. 

The lock on camera needs to be a bit higher as well.

This isn't an AMAZING 10/10 game but none of the Darksiders games are, 1 was a 8/10 and 2 was a 7/10 for me. This one is a very well put together game that feels great to play a solid 7.5/10.

Now that I've 100%-ed this game on the hardest difficulty I can safely say that it's definitely worth the try. At first it might seem different to the other Darksiders games but please, give it some time and try to get used to it, as it has slightly different mechanics. It grows quite a lot and you'll probably like it a lot later on when you unlock more and more stuff.

After some time it even became my most played game of the series (saying this while I ABSOLUTELY LOVED the 1st and 2nd game and had beaten them multiple times as well). It has a lot of variety of gameplay. Different choices throughout each playthrough make this one quite a fun ride.
Visually stunning, different areas give completely new vibes and the world itself is built quite well I'd say. Exploration is fun as there are quite a few secret areas with nice rewards. Boss fights on the highest difficulty are challenging at your first encounter with them but may vary from difficulty to difficulty (I started the game on Reckoning so it adds more to the fun and challenge).

I also recommend getting both the DLCs because they add quite a lot to the game. I won't go too much into detail about that in order not to spoil the fun of the exploration.

There are a few small bugs but nothing to worry about too much. One annoying bug is the fact that sometimes you're unable to use consumables mid-battle and it may kill you. Happens rarely.

[h1] Horseless Horseman [/h1]
Like a phoenix from the ashes, Darksiders franchise has risen from the dead following the acquisition of THQ by Nordic Games. The third instalment of the series depicts a tale of Fury, one of the four horsemen of the apocalypse, sent to hunt down powerful demons known as the seven deadly sins. Being an avid fan of the first two games I was more than happy to once again see my favourite depiction of the biblical horsemen. However, for all the pretty notions of “the miracle of life” - the act of birth itself is a rather nasty business. The first steps of Darksiders 3 were much more alike those of a toddler than the mythical fiery bird. After a messy launch it took the developers time, plenty of performance patches and 2 DLCs to raise the newborn Darksiders into a game it is today. In short, the title in question is a decent action game in itself, albeit one that falls flat in comparison to the rest of the Darksiders franchise. 

[b] Vulgrim’s fireplace [/b]
When it comes to the long answer as to why Darksiders 3 is an odd one out, perhaps the best place to begin is the fact that the game can be accurately described as “soulslike”. What will immediately draw the attention of the franchise veterans is a significantly different combat system. Now it relies heavily on dodges which, when timed well, allow the player to perform a powerful counterattack. Furthermore, Fury’s simplistic moveset forces her to single-out enemies, forcing a much more methodical approach to combat. No more hurling the Horseman into the heat of battle and decimating groups of foes with devastating combos. Now a group of 3 sturdier enemies may prove a deadly threat. Moreover, take note that the game’s primary currency of souls is now used foremost to level up your character; and needs to be spent at the trader. The souls are also lost on the player’s death, but may be retrieved from the place where you met your end. Let’s just sprinkle on top the fact that the game is now only saved upon reaching one of Vulgrim’s serpent holes, requiring the player to replay significant parts of the level after dying and note that primary healing item is an upgradable trinket – Nephilim’s respite (not-an-estus™). The above doesn’t make the game bad, however it does paint a picture of severe identity crisis.

[b] Redemption Arc [/b]
Storywise, Darksiders 3 feels more at home. Called forth by the Charred Council, Fury is sent to eliminate the latest threat, capable of tipping the balance in the endless war between heavens and hell – the seven deadly sins. Taking place shortly before the main events of the first Darksiders, Fury’s mission takes her to a post-apocalyptic Earth. Basic familiarity with Wrath’s chapter of the story is strongly recommendable for context, as Darksiders 3’s plot is for the most part confusing mess.

An example of how the events tend to unfold in Darksiders 3 should speak volumes for itself. At early stage of the game Fury summons her steed, Rampage, only to find it writhing in agony from multiple angelic lances piercing its hide. As Fury watches in horror, her enemy uses the confusion to deal her a grievous blow, only for the broken horseman to get whisked away into a magical portal. A mysterious Lord of the Hollows reveals himself and straight-up tells Fury that she’s being used as a mere pawn - now serving as an enforcer of the council, not the balance her superiors are supposed to uphold. Fury brushes off the blunt piece of exposition as ridiculous. In response, Lord of the Hollows develops a habit of “randomly” summoning Fury, bestowing the now horseless rider with elemental powers and wooing her back into the action, conveniently equipped with means to progress the game. Oh, and Rampage? Fury brings up the matter in a single conversation and the plot thread is dropped there, unresolved. 

What I mean to highlight with the scene above is how Darksiders 3 repeatedly appears to set up events and characters as far more relevant than they eventually turn out to be. To make matters worse, Fury begins the game as a painfully uncompelling character. True to her name, she’s moody and impetuous, in a manner unbecoming of her station. The reoccurring theme of redemption, involved with horsemen quests, in case of Fury is conquering her bad temper. To the game’s credit, it has a surprisingly decent ending, which really takes by surprise considering to how silly most of the plot is. If only it didn’t include a mysterious trinket that everyone allegedly knows about, short only of Fury and the player. Over and over again, the story is all setup and no pay-off.

[b] Two steps forward, one step back [/b]
Reception of Dark Souls inspirations is a matter of taste and some may forgive story shenanigans in an action game. Truth be told, the core gameplay of this title is positively decent. Tailored around new combat system, the fighting does feel satisfying once you get used to it. Especially numerous and varied encounters with the bosses are the definite highlight of Darksiders 3, providing both a challenge and a jolt of adrenaline. The game heavily encourages exploration, inviting player to revisit areas after acquisition of new powers as to reach new secrets filled with loot. Playing a gatherer proved a surprisingly fun way to fill time between the fights, as environmental puzzles are extremely downplayed in Darksiders 3 to the point they no longer play this part. 

Sadly, the second you begin to consider this title as part of the series, it all becomes a downward spiral. Those familiar with previous games may as well forget that Darksiders 2 ever happened. Any notions of an open world, the grand scale, RPG-like loot system are well out of the window. Comparable only to the first game, Darksiders 3 prefers its environment up-close and personal. The entirety of the game takes place exclusively on the ravaged Earth, considerably downplaying biblical inspirations and aesthetic that should be the staple of the game. To make matters worse, the game consistently uses the models from the previous two titles, perhaps the most obnoxious example of recycling being Darksiders 2’s arena made into a DLC in the third game. It is fun to play, however seeing what used to be part of base game sold separately just nails the coffin. In Darksiders 3 defence, the puzzle-centred Keepers of the Void DLC does prove that you could get inventive with Fury’s powers, and delivers by far the best bossfight of the game. It’s a shame that it takes extra content to experience this variety, sorely missing from the base game. No matter how you look at it, as a part of a franchise, Darksiders 3 is a step back in almost every regard.

[b] Beating the dead horse [/b]
Closing summary of Darksiders 3 proved to be unusually conflicted task, as the game left me with extremely mixed impressions. Despite all the criticism I have for the Fury’s chapter, I did enjoy this title. It is a fun action piece, fully capable of delivering several evenings worth of a good time. This would normally earn the game a “reluctant pass” mark, although I do struggle to find an audience I could genuinely recommend this game to. Being a sequel, it would normally be the fans of the franchise, however Darksiders 3 is foremost guilty by association – decent as it may be, the game fails to meet the high standard established by its predecessors. In fact, the fans of series are the ones most likely to get disappointed. Those among you starved for more Darksiders content and prepared to keep your expectations low, should however find this title a safe bet. I have no regrets about time spent with Fury’s whipping frenzy, which doesn’t change the fact Darksiders 3 is just a bad sequel.

This Review is from after i done my 100% Achievement Run on apocalyptic on first playthrough (~19-20 ingame hours) and i had a lot of fun, great game, i will play it again.
(review is from the 29.nov.2018, at game version 1.03)

[b]In terms of graphics:[/b]
i edited C:\Users\username\AppData\Local\Darksiders3\Saved\Config\WindowsNoEditor\GameUserSettings.txt and set sg.ResolutionQuality to 100 for sharper textures, because it was only at 71, even if ingame setting are on epic. foliage quality and antialaisin on high, everything else on epic with an 980gtx. Game runs smooth and i had only 2-3 frame drops in the second last area before the end. 
(edit: first set ingame settings and after that edit/control the file)

[b]Pro:[/b]
- Graphics / Artstyle / visual Effects
- Soundtrack is great
- Soundeffects are nice
- Enemy Design / Animations
- Story is okay, which brings the global game series story further (okay = not boring :P)
- Gameplay very fluid and i had a lot of fun with the dodging mechanic and combo system

[b]Neutral:[/b]
- You cant remap Controller and dont have another Preset (29.11.2018) And Dodge is on RB. i had a hard time getting used to, because so many other games have attack, special attack or usable items on rb. But after a while it was fine and control mapping feel fine.

[b]Contra:[/b]
- i dont have a contra point. game runs smooth without bugs (config thing is a bug, yes, but its easy to edit) and i had no trouble with camera (i used lock on only on bosses) and apocalytic difficulty felt great. maybe a little bit to easy further in the game, when you have alot of levels and upgrades and if you are better in the game in terms of doing the perfect dodges for slowmo+more damage

[b]Comparison:[/b]
I dont like comparisons, because it still feel like a Darksiders, because of Artstyle, Combat, Story and overall Gameplay exploration wise. But if you wanna do a comparison, then it feels like a combination of Darksiders 1 than 2 with some new gameplay additions and some less. i personaly dont liked the random loot rpg system from 2, so its a pro point for me that the upgrade system is more like the first one and the skilltree was replaced with different stances with there own combos and mechanics, so the game focus is more on exploration and combat than on manage inventory stuff. 
its not like Dark Souls, like other reviews say. Dark Souls have a way clunkier combat system and is not an metroidvania nor an hack'n'slash game. If you dont played Darksiders 1 and/or 2, and you want to compare it to something else, than you can compare it with Devil May Cry for the combat feeling and Hollow Knight, but in 3d, for the Metroidvania exploration feeling.

i dont get it, why games like dark souls, nioh, bloodborne, death gambit, hollow knight get the difficulty as a "pro" point, but this game here gets so much hate for it even if it have difficulty settings and story mode is rly a story mode no joke, which those games dont have. and darksiders1+2 had the same difficulty levels as this game here and they had the same combo system, even the dodge mechanic was slightly the same.

Really liked this game, one of my favorites. I think almost all the negative reviews are due to missed expectations - the gameplay has nothing to do with the previous Darksiders games, and instead resembles Dark Souls.

However, it's missing some very frustrating aspects of souls-likes:
- You don't lose souls (souls are dropped when you die, but you can pick them up after as many deaths as you like. kinda weird to lose them in the first place). An exception is the final boss battle - wish I knew this before going into it.
- You can pause or quit the game any time.
- There are checkpoints right next to most of the bosses. A couple are pretty far, but those bosses are not the hardest ones. So you don't spend most of the game running from a checkpoint between boss tries.

I played the whole thing on the hardest difficulty (Reckoning) and it was a blast. Some very satisfying moments when you learn all the boss' attack patterns and after many tries finally beat him (almost) flawlessly. I didn't get bored at all until after NG+ (btw, there is NG+9 if you absolutely love the game). Other notes:

- The world is beautiful and interconnected.
- Story is okay, not worse than previous Darksiders games; there is even some character development.
- Music is good.
- Hard to forget the main villains because you already know them (the Seven Deadly Sins)
- Feeling of character progression. Every upgrade matters, things like +20% health might go unnoticeable in some other games, but here it's a game changer (again, might be specific to Reckoning difficulty)
- The DLCs are a mixed bag - I liked Keepers of the Void (especially the final boss), but not the Crucible (used my potions to complete it as quick as possible and never touch again).
- My only real grudge is a bug with not saving progress. I lost 2+ hours of progress because of that. As far as I know though, it only happens in a specific place ([spoiler] if you die during the Angelic Champion fight [/spoiler]), so you just need to reload the game when you do that.

All in all, should definitely try if you like souls-like, but want a more forgiving game. If you are here for Darksiders - I don't know, it's a pretty different game; can probably complete it easily on a lower difficulty, but I can see how that could be boring.

Finished the game in balanced difficulty mode. Time to make a review.

Let me make this point clear. [b]ITS [u]NOT[/u] THE GENERIC HACK N SLASH [/b]that DS 1 & 2 was. If that’s what you are after, then this game is not for you.
We need to keep in mind that this is developed by a new studio and cannot expect it to be like how the series was before. Sure it uses concepts of dark souls like serpent holes for saving/fast travel , dropping  souls on death, but improvises it with its own system of combining concepts from Darksouls and Bayonetta .

[b]COMBAT:[/b]
The lock aim camera is useless when facing multiple enemies. So its better to just manually combat instead with mouse/controller movements. The camera angle or screen view distance certainly needs a change.
Learn the arcane counter since the combat system in DS3 is changed to the likes of bayonetta which uses witch time as a counter, here we use arcane counter. This is a life saving ability that makes combat easier.
Enemies are scripted in way they ambush you. So never run wild, look out for enemies before entering any new place. They can be hanging by the ceiling, hiding in the closet or even cloaked.  They all got a growling sound to give away their presence of being nearby. So be cautious and be prepared or pay for the mistake. You can make use of the various hollow weapons to make great combos with synergy to each weapon. 

[b]LORE & GRAPHICS:[/b]
The lore is pretty much the post boss cut scene and final cut scene in the game. In short it’s nonexistent. It is not story rich like its predecessors.
Graphics is beautiful and follows the same style of the previous Darksiders. The underwater levels are one of the best arts in the game. It’s colorful and vivid.

[b]GAMEPLAY:[/b]
There is no map. Yes, the beautiful detailed maps of the previous games especially DS2 is no longer in this one. Sure they took the souls approach and its fine but, there is a compass which is pretty much useless. Remove it and we can still play the game like normal.
As a fan of the first two games I expected a lot of puzzles and platforming. Sadly it was  disappointing.
It’s more of a run around the place to release a lever to progress to the next level. It has hardly any good puzzles when compared to its predecessor.
The music score is definitely good with really good transition to attacks and ambient sounds. Nothing is too much and too little. 
The game play was smooth without any noticeable stutter or FPS drop at EPIC settings @1080p/60 fps.
There was one crash in my whole game play in the scar region.

[b]VERDICT:[/b]
As a third installment to the series, it’s supposed to follow the series or improve upon it but not change a little too much. Unfortunately Darksiders 3 is a victim of its own change. I would rate it 7/10.

As a standalone game where this is not tied to the previous games, making this the first, then everything changes. In short without any prior expectations to the game and accepting the game for what it is, I would rate it 8.5/10.

It all comes down to how much [b]FUN[/b] was the game.
Was is mind-blowing? [b]NO[/b]
Was it boring? [b]NO[/b]
Was it satisfying? [b]YES[/b]
Would I replay it? [b]YES[/b]

Thank you for reading my review. Hope it was helpful and I hope we get a better darksiders 4.

I really pains me to give this a not recommend, because it's not really a bad game, but it feels like a huge step back from previous titles in the series. I was a huge fan of previous titles in the series, which is why I got this one. 

There are some parts of the game which I enjoyed, such as:

>The story. This is what keeps me playing. I really like the story of the series, and I'm really keen to see how the saga continues/ends.

>The setting. I've always been a sucker for post-apocalyptic worlds, and this one really intrigues me. And they added HUMANS! Always wondered what happened to them, and they added them into the game.

>The Puzzles. Always fun. These were really well put together, and sometimes a little difficult. which I liked.

However, there was also a lot of bad things about this game. Some of which were downright infuriating:

I'm a long time fan of the Darksiders series since the first game. Even back then, I fully understood that the series suffered from an identity issue but it wasn't something that really bothered me because I felt it executed those game mechanics it draws from other games pretty well. In short, it's always been a metroid-vania style game where you had a big dungeon complex, a map of it, and treasure/tools you get along the way to traverse and get past puzzles to get to bosses and even more trasure, all of those with a coat of paint from its pretty neat universe, awesome art from Joe Mad, and an action adventure style combat reminiscent of God of War/Devil May Cry.

Over time, the devs have always added or tweaked things with some parts of their formula. For instance in Darksiders 2, they added an RPG system that emphasised loot and a skill tree on top of their existing systems. In my opinion it worked for the most part. I personally didn't like their loot system because it created bloat and tended to slow down the flow of gameplay with loot management where the majority of loot was worthless. 

With Darksiders 3, the core of the series is still there but they tweaked the gameplay design to be much more similar to Dark Souls in terms of how you're supposed to approach engagements and how punishing every enemy can be, made even worse if you're forced to engage a large group of them at the same time. The similarities doesn't end there. The overall map design is heavily inspired by the Soulbourne series where you have many different locales that are interconnected through natural progression and unlocked "shortcuts". The boss design is much more grounded and takes emphasis away from spectacle and focuses more on perfect execution of dodging machanics and punishing/whittling the bosses down with jabs in between. 

Don't get me wrong, Dark Souls didn't invent difficulty or these design decisions but it did iterate on them to the point of near perfection garnering its own sub-genre and cult following, but Darksiders 3 kind of misses certain aspects of what makes that sub-genre work and thus it kind of hurts the game. When people point out it's a Dark Souls clone in a negative light, they're not completely wrong. They're just pointing out what's most apparent to them and I think there's more to that statement that's just not being said. I think we can all agree that Darksiders 3 is similar enough to the Soulsbourne games to warrant a comparison, and if you staunchly disagree with that I don't know what else to tell you other then I think you're either being willfully ignorant or dishonest. 

On top of the numerous technical faults the game has such as FPS loss in larger open areas, wonky dodge and terrain traversal, occasional crashing, and very weird duel monitor support where it defaults to the second screen, from what I can name off the top of my head as of writing this anyway, I think the games two biggest issues are its enemy designs and how non-commital the game is when it comes to what it's intented to be.

In terms of enemy design, I think the grunts need to be way less punishing. They're grunts, meant to be a minor hinderance to get to the next area/boss. Keep in mind there is significant power creep in this game outside of bosses as far as I'm aware, but it did take some time to get to that point where I can essentially two shot all but the toughest of enemies. What makes Dark Souls enemy design great is how tough but fair they feel, many of which has wind up times or very clear indications that they're about to strike and the player must respond approriately. Darksiders 3 enemies feel cheap to me. Outside of the lowliest grunts you have enemies that block and they're infuriating to fight, even worse when there's more than one or the shielding enemy also has a massive health pool as well. The only thing to do at this point is to either wind up a power attack from your hollow weapon, which leaves you open for a quick attack on you, or to wait for an opening to do a mix up or arcane counter. These solutions do not feel good to play because they essentially force you to wait or make an engagement far more tedious than necessary and this design extends to some boss encounters as well such as Avarice. This to me is cheap or it creates artificial difficulty which I hate.  That's without mentioning that learning when to dodge can be tricky as well especially when enemies have some form of AoE attack because you have to dodge when they impact the ground or near your character as opposed to when their weapon is about to colide with your character's model. Also numerous enemies can stunlock you which is another annoying things about their enemies.

Much like Dark Souls it has soul clusters that you can accumulate in your inventory and break if you need a boost in souls, the in-game currency. However the soul mechanic has no risk associated with it in this game because when you die, the souls you drop never disappear and can be retrieved whenever you want. So it makes me wonder why even have this mechanic in the first place?

So where does Darksiders 3 shine then? I think visually, it's kept most of the flair and style of the last two games. I'd still prefer if Fury kept her original comic design, or at least make it an option, but this current one grew on me. I just think the whole angry red-headed woman fighter archetype is a tired trope. The story, while not devoid of flaws, I think did a decent enough job but it took more than halfway through the game to realize this. Early on, I really didn't like Fury's characterization/motivation and voice because it seemed to clash so much with Death and War. War was on a quest to clear his name and find the ones responsible for unleashing the Apocalypse. Death was on a quest to clear his brother's name by undoing the damage of the Apocalypse. Fury is out to kill seven very powerful demons because the Charred Council told her to in exchange for a title to lead the four... I know she's her own character, but keep in mind that these four Nephilim are the very last of their kind with a long history and judging by the last two games, I'd think they all deeply cared about one another at least and Fury just came off as a raging bitch for no reason lol (btw that's not a spoiler, you learn that in the very first cinematic)

Overtime, the combat got better as I learned the enemies and pre-patch that's just how the game is. It's not exactly my cup of tea or what I expected from a Darksiders game, hell I'm not even afan of Soulsbourne games but I can still apreciate them for what they are. As a fan of the Darksiders games, I'd recommend it at about 40-45 dollars. That to me would be a fair price for what we're getting here as is.
Not the Darksiders I was expecting but we got to see Fury on Fire.

Loved Darksiders 1 and 2.  Could barely put either of them down.

Darksiders 3 tries too hard to be Dark Souls, and it fails hard.  Part of what made Darksiders so much fun was feeling like an actual minor deity stomping around chasing down a puzzle.  Darksiders 3 feels like i spend more time fighting the game mechanics than stomping on bad guys.

I went into Darksiders III with low expectations because I didn’t enjoy Darksiders II… and came out genuinely surprised.

This game is a souls-lite gem.

If you’re someone who enjoys Souls combat but doesn’t want to deal with overwhelming systems or massive open-world chaos, this hits a really sweet spot. It’s focused, challenging, and respects your time. A lot of negative reviews come from older fans expecting Darksiders II again. They saw a souls-like shift and started complaining. To them, I’ll just say it straight, [b] skill issue. [/b]

The map design is where the game really hooked me. It’s not open-world, but an interconnected web of areas that loop back into each other in a really satisfying way. I usually don’t like metroidvania-style backtracking, but here it felt purposeful. Every time I unlocked a new Hollow power, I immediately remembered places I couldn’t reach before and actually wanted to go back. That curiosity kept pulling me forward.

Exploration is backed by smart puzzle design. Each area has multiple puzzles that make you stop and think, and they never feel random. The mechanics are clean, and traversal stays simple even when the world itself is complex. The Hollow abilities (Flame, Storm, etc.) are a highlight. Each one changes both combat and movement in meaningful ways.

Combat is slower and more deliberate compared to previous Darksiders games, but that’s exactly why it works. It rewards patience and awareness instead of button mashing.

Now for the one thing that really annoyed me:
Those Prince of Persia-style swing sections. The same button is used for attacking and grappling, which leads to moments where you accidentally attack mid-air and fall. It’s frustrating and easily the weakest part of the gameplay.

And then there’s Fury.

Fury absolutely carries the experience. Ruthless, powerful, and commanding presence throughout. Her character arc is surprisingly well done, and yeah, At your service, my queen.

The story is structured, easy to follow without being hand-holdy, and ties nicely into the larger Darksiders universe. It left me actually interested in what comes next, especially with Darksiders 4 on the horizon.

[b] Overall: 9/10 [/b]

If you like Souls-like combat but want something more focused and manageable, this is a lightweight goldmine. Highly recommended.

I loved the Darksiders game when it first came out. Played it to death and back (pun not intended) and then again some. To me it was like reliving my childhood years on the N64 playing Zelda - similar dynamic with combat and puzzles, well balanced, with an element of free-reign exploration.

I waited for years for Darksiders 2 to come out - and it didn't disappoint. I really enjoyed the RPG elements like gear swapping and deciding whether you're a caster or melee dps. It was just a generally well refined game - smooth in every sense.

Darksiders 3 is kind of like those games. But it really kind of isn't.  The targetting system is a nightmare - you're as well just ignoring it, if not for the fact Fury's most effective dodge is while targetting a mob. But while targetting you've absolutely no idea what else is happening in the environment. And other than bosses, you will rarely be facing just ONE enemy - you'll target one and have two more completely offscreen, charging up attacks and smacking you without you having the faintest inkling.

I don't want to play Dark Souls. I want to play Darksiders.

Also you get a refillable flask. With a lengthy animation. That gets you killed half the time trying to heal. Sound familiar?

AND THE TRAVELLING. MY GOD THE TRAVELLING. I've been fighting a boss now where every time it murderstomps me I'm having to walk the equivelant of a country mile to recollect my lost souls. Again that sounds crazy familiar.

THQ what the F*** have you done? Give me back my Gothic Zelda Murderfest! Your world building in this series is amazing and I love the story but you've annihilated the core mechanics!

Folks complain mainly about the change in the combat system. Well yes, they ditched the "PRESS X a million times to win" approach. I for one, love it!
- Now you got fewer enemies (who do hurt)
- Timing windows for your dodges
- Meaningful combo choices you can learn and master
- Audible and visual cues for enemy attacks
- An arrow in the screen center will show from what direction an unseen enemy (not on screen) attacks

These changes make the encounters skillbased, fair and way more interesting. You will approach the terrain careful while scanning enemy placement. Once engaged in combat you stay perceptive, furthermore remember room layout and from what angle other enemies will attack. You will pull enemies, crowd control and herd them, dodge them like bullets in "The Matrix" and unleash devastating counter attacks. Feels good!

Other nice things to know:
- Adjustable difficulty
- Little to no grind (you can, but dont have to)
- Game keeps you on track with an objective compass (instead of a minimap)
- Exploration is challenging but rewarding (...again - no minimap)
- Beautiful crafted levels.
- The world is "semi open". Fast travel points are mostly connected with levels that follow a certain path and you can unlock shortcuts to others. But you cannot hike a mountain like in Skyrim.
- Efficient fast travel system with unlockable stations
- Enemies respawn when you die, but NOT when you fast travel or unlock fast travel points
- Story, while not as epic as the first part (what an ending!!), is above the cringeworthy second entry to the franchise who relied mostly on the word "Nephilim" to be repeated like a broken record.

What i dislike is the lack of a proper tutorial. Screen prompts do show when you have absolutely no time to read them ... like during your first boss fight, and are then gone forever. Some important things (like the button to toggle "run" are not even mentioned.)
Your healing powers are cost free replenished only in combat or when you die, thus making it a viable strategy to kill yourself next to a fast travel point. Viable but immersion killing.
Price is too steep, especially with the Deluxe Edition (the DLC is meh).

But minor annoyances aside. A very good game. Go for it on sale and if you are up for a challenge.

P.S. The game is clearly designed to be played with gamepad and I do. I don't know if the K+M controls are any good.

I can't think of a more accurate way to describe this game than by calling it "aggressively mediocre". It's the mother of all 6/10 games. In a vacuum, Darksiders 3 is a good game. The problem is that there are so many other games available that do everything this game does better, with the most obvious among these (by far) is Dark Souls.  Here's a list of "souls-like" aspects this game has off the top of my head:

1. Die and you lose your souls but you can reclaim them on respawn. 
2. Experience is actually called souls, and there's a little soul counter at the bottom right of the screen.
3. Most of the loot you pick up are useable soul items (called lurchers). 
4. Bonfires are out and Vulgrim is in. You level up and teleport at Vulgrim's little spots and the teleport menu is exactly like Dark Souls 3.
5. The adamantite weapon upgrade system functions the same as titanite upgrades, no exaggeration. Adamantite slivers will upgrade a weapon to level 3, fragments to level 6, pieces to level 9, and one adamantite chunk upgrades it to level 10. 
6. Big ol' health bar for bosses at the bottom of the screen
7. Souls are also your currency to buy stuff from Vulgrim.
8. Some of the areas have shortcuts you unlock once you do the full area.
9. Interconnected world.

Anyways, here's the obligatory Steam review pros and cons.

Pros:
+  Fury's voice acting is phenomenal. While people seem to be divided on whether or not they actually like her as a character, I personally thought she was great.
+  There are lots of metroidvania aspects (possibly too many), like different abilities opening different doors that you can backtrack to later.
+  Some of the boss fights are fun.
+  Interconnected world.

Cons:
-  The metroidvania aspects aren't quite as rewarding since there's only a small handful of possible items you can find, most of which being the useable soul items (lurchers).

-  The interconnected world is a good thing but since Vulgrim has so many locations, and the fact that so many areas look the same, the concept of an interconnected world loses it's appeal and utility. 

-  There is no map of the world and it certainly would have been nice to have one. I'm assuming the mentality behind this decision was the idea of having an interconnected world would make maps redundant. Dark Souls didn't have a map but it didn't need one because of how distinct each area looked. This made it much easier to remember locations. There is a compass at the top of the screen that kind of works, for what its worth. 

-  Unintuitive UI. If I want to use a lurcher item, I have to press the following sequence of buttons to get to the screen they're on: Start, R2, R1, R1, R1. This is so unnecessary considering how much dead space there is on each menu screen as well as how large the text and graphics are on each screen.

-  The camera is not very reliable. If you lock onto an enemy, for whatever reason the camera moves down to the battlefield, behind Fury, thus making it hard to see the enemy you just targeted, or anything else in front of her. I have no idea why it doesn't just stay in the air. Also, the camera doesn't move further away from Fury if she's getting attacked by multiple enemies at once. This means that you're going to get hit by enemies off screen all the time and since there's no block button, you'll probably end up mashing dodge when this happens. There is an on-screen notifier that will point in the direction of an incoming attack, but it's so subtle in its presentation that I didn't even notice it until I was almost half way into the game. 

-  The combat, while fluid and responsive, still feels somewhat off. It really feels like the developer couldn't decide if they wanted a more one on one approach with combat, similar to Dark Souls, or a more traditional hack and slash gameplay similar to this franchise's previous titles. I started the game on "Challenging" difficulty, but ended up lowering it due to all the frustrating off-screen attacks that I couldn't see.
 
-  There's no way to remap your controller buttons (though you can for keyboard and mouse). This should be a standard option in games these days but it's even worse in this game due to the strange default button mapping. For example, the dodge button is not Circle or B or anything else you're probably used to. It's R1. Why in the world is it R1 and why can't I change it? I'm almost at the end of the game and I'm still hitting circle to dodge on accident.

-  About midway through the game and on, the enemies will start delaying their attacks, screwing up your dodge timing in the process (remember, there's no block in this game). Lots of games, particularly souls-like games do this, and it's just such a lazy attempt at adding challenge, imo.

I went into this game as a loyal Darksiders fan (played through 1 and 2 several times on pretty much every difficulty).

The first thing I noticed was pretty minor but still off-putting: Right away the menu system is a bit of a mess. The first button you mouse over is highlighted and then when you move your mouse to a different button the previous one is still highlighted, so you never know what the heck you're clicking. I restarted but it stayed the same. 

After blindly clicking past the menus and selecting what I think was the "challenging" difficulty mode, I was greeted with a lovely illustrated cinematic and then another cinematic showing Fury in-game next to her horse, which was HORRENDOUSLY crunchy. As soon as I could, I dialed up the anti-aliasing (all the graphics settings started on low) which then made everything extremely blurry. I increased all the other graphics settings hoping that it was the texture quality, to no avail. When I restarted for the 2nd time though, it resolved itself.

Now finally able to enjoy the incredibly beautiful graphics the game had to offer (I mean really, this game is PRETTY), I made my way to the first boss. The dialogue was entertaining, and I really do like Fury's personality, although the Watcher is like toting around a puppy compared to the one from DS1 and feels a bit pointless. 

The game stayed pretty entertaining until Vulgrim showed up, and then it took a nosedive. This wasn't because of Vulgrim himself (he is one of my favorite characters of the series) but because of the introduction of the "attribute point" system. Basically your character now levels up somewhat manually by feeding souls to Vulgrim rather than earning EXP from killing mobs. This idea could have worked, but MAN the ways you can spend your level-up attribute points are DRY AS HELL. Either you get a 20hp increase, a 5% damage increase, or a 7% arcane damage increase. Excuse me? What happened to the cool talent trees from DS2? You can't even feel these increases at all anyway, so it feels so pointless. 

As the game continued, it became extremely punishing (sends you back to the last Vulgrim location every time you die, and straight-up doesn't let you save your game). Fury has next to no health, and a 20hp increase per attribute point is laughable.  It isn't that the combat is particularly difficult either, just that it is clunky and hindered by bad game mechanics. For instance, to use your "nephilim's respite" (the equivalent of a refillable health potion that gets restored from green souls) you have to be a country mile away from your enemy or else they're just going to murder you while you use it. The thing has an animation that takes about a million years where you can't move or dodge attacks so you're just sitting there drinking goo while you get your face kicked in. It is infuriating after a couple hours into the game.

The game tries its hardest to throw familiar faces at you (War, Vulgrim, Ulthane, etc) but apart from that and the architecture, the game feels like a distant cousin to the first two games, and not in a good way. Execute animations are gone. Combos are toned way down. There's no satisfying gear to loot or anything, and instead the only loot you get are just globs of souls that get sent to your inventory to be used in front of Vulgrim so you don't lose them when you die.  

Conclusion: This is the "Mass Effect Andromeda" of the Darksiders series. Graphically amazing, but otherwise a complete mess that doesn't belong in the series. It's hindered by lackluster character progression, extremely poor combat mechanics, the inability to save your game manually, and a bad first impression due to the glitchy as heck menus. Moral of the story: Don't fix what ain't broken. The devs should have stuck with what worked from the first two games.

Darksiders 3 is the souls-lite version of the Darksiders series, replacing the Zelda gameplay of the first and Prince of Persia style of the second with a large interconnected world and the need for well timed dodges and counter attacks. I don’t think I have ever played a series that changes gameplay as well as the Darksiders series. If you like souls like games, being punished for button mashing or games that require twitch like reaction speeds in combat then Darksiders 3 is for you. 

One thing Darksiders excelled at telling the same story from different point of views. If you were hoping DS3 was going to continue the story from where the first game ended then prepare to be disappointed. Starting 10 years after the prologue of the first game (and finishing somewhere before the end of the second game and before war is sent back to earth in the first) you take control of Fury, the 3rd horsemen. Disdainful of her fellow riders and full of anger and boredom she is summoned by the charred counsel to capture the 7 sins, monstrous beings that are the embodiment of their traits, that serve neither heaven or hell but will still destroy the balance if left unchecked.  What starts off as a simple story of hunting down the sins turns into a very decent story of betrayal and provides tons of character growth as Fury slowly comes to see the flaws of the sins in herself and has to grow to overcome them, least she succumbs to them. This also changes her view on her fellow riders, characters from the other races and humanity itself.

Gameplay is been completely changed compared to the previous 2 games. Being a souls like game, death comes often and quickly, with basic enemies being able to kills you with a few hits. Using items has a cool down and takes item to use in game, which can be interrupted. The game is slightly more forgiving as there aren’t many enemies that hide behind object or behind blind corners, so if you are somewhat coordinated those death don’t happen all that frequently. Death when does happen will put you back at the last serpent hole point you were at and drop all your souls (currency). Unlike most game failing to collect these straight after your death doesn’t make you lose them- they hang around until you pick them up making it much more forgiving. You don’t have a stamina bar and can dodge to your hearts content. Souls are used for upgrading your level, with only 3 stats, health, physical and arcane damage being available. Each increase to one of these provides diminishing returns, and while tempting to dump all into 1 stat it’s good to at least upgrade semi evenly for a while so you don’t end up as a glass cannon. Weapons and eventually armour can also be upgraded for slight increases in stats or buffs, but the big buffs come from enhancements you can place in each weapon that provide active and passive bonuses.

The world is designed very well, with what is initially a liner path somewhat giving you an option of where to explore and who to fight before again becoming a fixed route at the end. The game does very little to show you where you have to go, with the only help bring a icon the points you to the closet sin(and the path to get to it). You don’t have to follow this, and exploring often rewards you with more collectables and items. After unlocking all the powers the game truly opens up, showing you just how connected the world is (it’s like a giant honeycomb). There are tons of secrets and extra places to explore if you can find the time. There are a fair few puzzle you have to solve, with the throwing bugs being some of the most annoying mini games I have played in a while.

The combat and enemies are well done, with each enemy being unique (no reused skins in here) and having a tell that advises when an attacking is coming. Just mashing the attack button will get you killed quickly, with the game rewarding perfect dodges that usually do a lot more damage and leave the enemy open for a few more attacks. You have a good choice of weapons, from your basic whip to each of the hollow infused forms that provide their own special moves and charged attacks. While the extra weapons won’t really help that much in combat it’s nice to be able to set enemies on fire or use a force attack to break the guard if blocking’s enemies. You have a wrath attack that changes depending on which power is selected that can easily help in combat, and the havoc mode where you can destroy anything that stands in your way for a short amount of time. The boss fights were outstanding, really bringing home the mechanics of the game and unforgiving if you forget them. Each of the bosses has great dialogue as they try and temp fury (I loved Sloth, Wrath and Lust), and the multipart fights were a good challenge. First time around I thought they were very difficult, but after respecting my stats and with a bit more practice I breezed through them a second time.

The voice work and cinematics were very good. Fury’s VA does a good job conveying her constant anger, and through it her growth central to the story. Other major supporting characters and bosses are also given a good amount of screen time and I loved the scenes where each of the sins try and tempt fury. The background music fit the game well, never overshadowing the dialogue or sound effects, but supporting the game from the background. The game does have a lot of pauses (either with in game cinematics or set movies) that introduce new bosses, concepts or character growth. For some reason the text in the cinematics doesn’t carry across in the screenshots in the base game, but works in the DLC.

The DLCs are a mixed bag. Both add new armours (which the crucible armour being helpful while The Voids abysmal armour is the best in game and should be your go to). The crucible is a easier version of what was in Darksiders 2, this time with plenty of mob rounds where you can replenish health, wrath and fury for the upcoming fights. By the time you have unlocked all of the fights it’s already endgame content, but the rewards might be able to help you get items and upgrades that you missed during the main play through. The Voids it more of a puzzle orientated dungeon, which you have to use each of the force hollows to proceed, and they get progressively harder. It does provide 4 new weapons (so you can slot in unused enhancements for the passive buff bonus) which is a massive bonus. The bosses are tough compared to the rest of the boss fights (however build upon an attack pattern for the DLCs end boss). The fight cinematics were quite funny, and not what I expected.

There is some replayability, with the option of a new game plus mode that gets increasingly more difficult to play, but nowhere near what was in The Surge. You do keep all your upgrades and items from previous play throughs, and while enemies are tougher to kill, you should already have a good handle on things. There is the options of changing combat to classic mode (items are used instantly and attacks don’t interrupt you)

If you are chasing 100% achievements then you will need to purchase both the DLC’s and grind a bit, as it requires at least 2 playthoughs, but it’s fairly easy to do and much more forgiving than other souls like games.
