Finished the game on **Reckoning difficulty. Don't do that.**

If you want a real challenge, play on **Apocalyptic**. Reckoning is less "difficult" and more "unfair". Most mid-game enemies can one or two-shot you while having enormous HP pools. One of the DLC bosses has over **200K HP**, while my whip combo was doing around 1K damage. That's not difficulty, that's just making the numbers bigger.

### What it does well

**Level Design — 9/10**

Probably the best part of the game. The world is beautifully interconnected, with great Metroidvania progression and verticality. Some areas genuinely reminded me of Dark Souls 1's Lordran and Dishonored. Skar, one of the final areas, is especially fun to explore once you have all the Hollows.

**Enemy & Boss Design — 8/10**

Darksiders has always had great enemy designs and III continues that tradition. The Seven Deadly Sins are visually great and most have interesting mechanics. Sloth is terrible, though. The Ionos fight from *Keepers of the Void*, on the other hand, is one of my favorite boss fights in the game.

**Story — 6/10**

Nothing special, nowhere near Darksiders I or II, but good enough to keep you going. Fury's character development comes a little too late. The good thing is that the game has very little padding. If you're here for the lore, play on Story difficulty and rush through the Seven Deadly Sins.

### What it does badly

**Combat — 4/10**

This is where the Soulslike approach completely falls apart.

Combat is basically:

**Wait for attack → dodge → Arcane Counter → repeat.**

You have normal attacks, charged attacks, Arcane Counters and a few Hollow abilities. That's about it. There are no meaningful combos, launchers, juggling, air combos or other mechanics that made previous Darksiders games fun.

Good Soulslikes give you multiple ways to approach an encounter. Darksiders III mostly gives you one: dodge and counter.

**Progression — 5/10**

You basically have three stats: Health, Physical Damage and Arcane Damage. There isn't much build variety.

The Enchantment system is also unnecessarily grindy. Fully upgrading enchantments requires a huge amount of materials, pushing you toward Crucible farming.

**Reckoning — 2/10**

Reckoning makes almost every enemy a damage sponge while reducing your dodge i-frames. Many enemies can kill you in one or two hits.

This doesn't feel like a skill-based challenge. It feels like an endurance test.

And then there's the **Crucible**.

There are checkpoints every 25 stages, which is a cool system. But the secret boss **Wicked K** requires a 1–100 run without using those checkpoints. On Reckoning, that's an absurd grind. A no-hit run can take around 90 minutes.

I actually cleared the entire Crucible, but eventually gave up on the 1–100 Reckoning run. I finished the game, started NG+ on Story and planned to change the difficulty later. Then I discovered the Crucible is progression-locked in NG+ and I could only go to Stage 25.

At that point, I simply closed the game.

**6.5/10**

Darksiders III is not a bad game. It has **excellent level design, good enemy/boss design and decent lore**, but the combat and Reckoning difficulty seriously drag it down.

If you want to experience the story, play on **Normal/Story**.

If you want a challenge, play **Apocalyptic**.

**Don't play Reckoning unless you genuinely enjoy suffering.**

Well, this isn’t that great of a game, it doesn’t really succeed as a sequel to Darksiders 1 and 2, and it doesn’t really succeed on its own premise either, it just kind of exists between the two different game's design ideas.

Let’s just get on with it, it’s no secret that when Vigil Games envisioned Darksiders they took a lot of inspiration from The Legend of Zelda, and even though Darksiders 2 introduced RPG elements it retained its Zelda DNA, with the RPG elements having been built up around the Zelda core rather than influencing it a whole lot. Darksiders 3 on the hand, tries to fusion Zelda with Dark Souls on a much more intimate level, where they tried to build a core out of them, which didn’t really work out that well.

There are elements of the game wanting to be Dark Souls so much but failing in how tight and poorly optimised the dodge mechanic is, it wants you to lose currency and progress when you die, but it doesn’t want to give you useful or applicable “campfires”, it wants Zelda like abilities, but it also wants to tie them to combat on a much more fundamental level. There are a lot of things Darksiders 3 wants to achieve, it wants to satisfy returning fans of Darksiders 1 and 2, but it also want to appeal to a newer soulsborne fanbase, and it wants to give a satisfying difference from how War and Death plays, which it actually does pretty well, taking everything into consideration, Fury plays and acts very different from her siblings and displaces a personality wholly her own, which I’ll commend Gunfire Game for achieving. But other than that, it doesn’t really measure that well up to its predecessors.

Having seen the horsemen War and Death’s stories in the first two entries in the series, Fury is given centre stage in Darksiders 3 in a story that takes places before the events of the first game.

Visually Darksiders 3 will look familiar to veterans of the series and does a good job of replicating the slightly cartoonish/drawn style of the original games, whilst bringing it up to a modern standard. The environments are varied and range from overgrown ruined cities to dilapidated underground stations and volcanic caves, each with their own distinct character. There are also a broad variety of enemy types unique to these different areas as well as a number of challenging bosses.

The gameplay is a big departure from the original games however. While the first two were structured similarly to traditional Zelda games, the third is much more of a souls-like. Gone are the open worlds, complex dungeons and puzzles of the first two, which are replaced by a more linear world with shortcuts that enable backtracking. Side quests are also gone and a world map is also absent. The shady demonic merchant Vulgrim returns however as a fast travel/bonfire mechanic and means of cashing in souls to level Fury up. The combat system has been simplified and revolves around dodging and counterattacking and the challenging difficulty will result in frequent returns to the location of your last death to collect your belongings, much like in Dark Souls.

All in all Darksiders 3 is a reasonable souls-like, but the changes to the gameplay, lack of an open world and general dumbing down is likely to leave fans of the originals disappointed.

It's clear to me that they hoped to capitalize on the Soulsborne hype by copying many of the core mechanics from those titles. As a product of this, Darksiders 3 is a poor man's Dark Souls.

The concept of hunting down the 7 Sins is decent, but otherwise the story is rather uninspired and bland. There is a serious lack of new and original characters.
Original Darksiders 1 characters were: Samael, Abaddon, Lilith, Azrael, Ulthane, Uriel, Vulgrim, and The 5 Chosen.
Darksiders 3 has, what, Abraxis (Who appears once and has lit-er-ally no character development), Lord of Hollows, Usiel (who appears twice) and the 7 Sins? There's also 5 forgettable (and optional) Chosen, but I don't remember doing most of them. Otherwise there are many recurring characters, which is fine. But it shouldn't be a replacement for original characters.

Another thing which isn't a huge deal but kind of rubbed me the wrong way was the lack of over-the-top comical graphic violence that the series is otherwise known for. I remember watching War tear off Tiamat's wings, then doing a backflip mid-air while holding her severed wings, and then finally tearing out her still-beating heart in a fountain of blood while Tiamat screams in agony.

In Darksiders 3, by comparison, the most graphical thing I remember, is Fury catching an axe mid-air and throwing it back, hitting the target. Not a drop of blood to be seen. What a let-down.

4/10, would not recommend.

Now, the moment that gate opens... I crash. The moment I walk through it... I crash. The moment I pick up the Angelic Artifact behind the gate I crash. No matter what I do... I crash here, ALWAYS. So now.. I cannot progress the game whatsoever because I need to enter this room to get the sword.

I like this game, but it was different from the previous 2. For starters, you don't get to use your horse so your movement around the map will rely heavily on the Serpent Holes (teleportation) and travelling on foot. In terms of getting stronger, each level allows you to make your health, strength (basic attack damage), or arcane (other damage) higher and you are only allowed to pick 1. Your level doesn't rely on progression however which is nice, it's your choice to spend your currency on levels or other things like armour, temp boosts you can activate at specific times, or adamantine to upgrade your weapons (you can also find those temp boost shards and adamantine by exploring.  
Fury unlocks 4 different 'hollows' by playing which give her 4 extra different weapons to her standard whip and arcane effects of fire/extra jump, lightning/glide, guardbreak/magnetisation, and slowing/ice/ice walljumps. These are quite fun to play around with even if you will likely focus on upgrading 2 or 3 of the 5 to the max. 
While I had a lot of fun playing this and its dlcs and they had decent stories (not counting the crucible as it is just an arena), my only real dissapointment was the final guardian of the void. It was a real challenge for me and after many attempts I was finally ready when it broke and didn't move. I killed it but by that time I was too strong and good at the game that the last 3 bosses only required a single attempt each. I still had some extra temp boost shards and health flasks left over. Maybe that final guardian of the void dlc was too strong for the rest of the game, but it also wouldn't have made too much sense for me to do it any later than after 1 or 2 more boss as you enter the final act fighting the 2nd to last boss. 

TLDR; I had a fun time with a good story, but it was different to the previous 2 Darksiders games and I dissapointingly became too strong fighting a dlc boss for the end of the game.
